title: Sheeva Dragonsister
type: Zarathian operative, honored lady, and painter
dek: An honored operative who expects a life after hidden service, turns toward painting and mutual trust with Eugene, and later feels the cost of his absence.

facts.Public accomplishment: Discovery of captives being fed to dragons
facts.Later glimpse: Dreams of Eugene during his distant Babel expedition

sources: Zarathis_Dragonsisters_NPC_Master.md — supplied 5 October 2026; quest-RP parts 024, 026, 030 and explicit evidence distinctions
body:
Sheeva helped make a hidden operation into a public victory, but peace asks something different of her. One of the Dragonsisters, she expects a reprieve after years of service, speaks warmly of the country she protected and begins to make space for painting and Eugene. Her confidence, guarded history and need for mutual trust belong to the same person.

The hidden service becomes a public honor

At the celebration on 15, Month of Cala, Year 2, Captain Zythienne calls Sheeva, Kaiyah and Minyah before the crowd. He credits their years living among the enemy and singles out Sheeva for discovering that enslaved captives were being fed to dragons.

The sisters stand together as the state makes their contribution public. Sheeva is proud. The narrator later identifies her as their social leader and confirms that their closeness is sincere. That does not establish a formal command over her sisters.

Zythienne raises them to ladies of the lands and promises honor and care to their families. The ceremony establishes recognition, without supplying the estates, legal powers or succession rights attached to the title.

In a later conversation, Sheeva says their father had a reputation in the Emerald Veil and that they grew up with its principles before training for infiltration. This is her account of their family background. The father remains unnamed, and no verified ancestry or new family member is invented from it.

Eugene notices the reserve

At the July gathering, Eugene notices a masked, soldierly sister who lets others speak. The narrator suggests a battle scar beneath the mask. Later dialogue names the woman he waits for as Sheeva. Kaiya also normally wears a mask; that detail alone cannot distinguish the sisters or settle the origin of an injury.

When urgent matters pull Eugene away, he apologizes to Sheeva and asks her to wait before their planned leap. The record establishes his attention returning to her, without recovering a complete account of the leap itself.

Speaking to Olokun afterward, Sheeva calls Eugene a mysterious, shy vulpine and looks forward to seeing him again. She is willing to try to draw him out, but only if he opens up too. Even in this early interest, intimacy must travel in both directions.

The peace she hopes to live in

After the ceremony, Sheeva tells Olokun that the sisters’ job is done and that they will rest while others finish the fighting. She says they were trained for a different kind of service, not combat. Years of dangerous intelligence work should not be mistaken for an invented battlefield command.

She admires Aria as a war hero whose courage builds people up. Bowene may be wise, she says, but he is less exciting. Her affection explains something of Aria’s public stature without proving that the admired figure is right in every dispute.

She also resists the assumption that every member of the Veil is an aggressor. She speaks of negotiators and peacemakers and thinks a gentle heart can belong there, provided it learns guile. Her own service makes subtlety a form of civic work, not a reason to dismiss the people who perform it.

Painting a life after the war

At their reunion in the Month of Moirah, Eugene asks Lady Sheeva to dance. She greets him affectionately and says she missed him. When he minimizes what he has to tell, she asks about the Shadow Roads and his research. His intellectual life matters to her as well as his company.

She has been painting because she has heard it can heal the heart and mind. She brings out a picture of Eugene, the person occupying her thoughts, and teases him about the difficulty of capturing his eyes. It is her chosen work during a reprieve, not evidence that another person has cured her.

She suggests a future walk through the mysterious passage he studies, with his hand to hold, and later says she would like to leave the gathering with him. Those invitations establish interest and trust, not that either journey or a permanent partnership has already been completed.

Kaiya’s approval gives another view of the bond: she values Eugene’s humility and the dignity with which he treats her sister. Sheeva’s public honor and her private affection do not require the same kind of courage.

Comfort in a night of remembrance

At the memorial in the Month of Hope, Sheeva and Eugene greet each other warmly after another absence. He insists on first paying respects and offering condolences. She calls the act honorable, while he declines credit for an idea that was not his own.

Their teasing continues around Gartina’s food, but the evening becomes more demanding when the soldiers return. Eugene helps steady the frightened crowd, and the narrator explicitly says Sheeva is impressed by his leadership.

Sheeva also tries to help, watching to see whether he notices. The former hidden operative is present in the work of caring for people, not simply watching a romance unfold around her.

After the conflict and distress, she asks Eugene not to leave her alone that night. The request makes vulnerability visible beside confidence and flirtation. It establishes a need for trusted company, without declaring new vows or erasing the work she did before they met.

Faith across an absence

A later Babel quest moment, posted on 27, Month of Talan, Year 3, shows Sheeva dreaming of Eugene from far away. The scene names a feeling of abandonment alongside her faith that he will return a true hero.

It is a glimpse of her experience of distance, not proof that she has traveled with him, knows everything he is facing or receives a magical message from him. Earlier warmth has left an expectation that absence can hurt.

A life larger than its public legend

Sheeva’s history includes intelligence work, national recognition, admiration for Aria, an intended reprieve, painting and a meaningful mutual attachment with Eugene. Her service predates that attachment; the relationship cannot become the reason for every earlier choice.

Her age, ancestry, the origin of the apparent scar, the full record of her wartime experience and her eventual fate remain unrecovered. Her family account adds a claimed background without identifying her father. Marriage, betrothal, children, exclusivity, relocation and a completed reunion are not established.

Her sisters choose differently after the shared operation. Kaiya turns toward study, while Minyah prepares another mission. Their closeness survives without making their futures interchangeable.
